mainTopic: Birds that fall (surfaces and the glue-board), and when uprooted or broken ribs make an animal טרפה
overview: The גמרא finishes its list of surfaces a falling bird might land on. If the surface slips away under the bird, there is no worry of רסוק אברים; if it stays firm, there is. Next comes a bird stuck to a glue-board (דבוק). The two versions of the רב אשי and אמימר dispute lead to the ruling: two wings stuck is forbidden, one wing stuck is permitted. The גמרא then turns to the משנה's case of broken ribs. Twelve ribs make a majority, and זעירי and רבי יוחנן add limits on which breaks count. בן זכאי and רבי יוחנן argue over whether uprooted ribs need most of one side or most of both sides. רב rules that a rib uprooted with part of its vertebra is a טרפה, and that losing two opposite ribs of one vertebra is like an animal split in half (גיסטרא). A long back-and-forth explains these rulings and the way his students worded their question. The amud ends with שמואל's three cases of טרפה and a challenge to his rib ruling, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Sand, road dust, and straw
steps.stepSummary: Fine sand and loose straw raise no worry. Coarse sand, road dust and bundled straw do raise a worry of רסוק אברים.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the bird fell on fine sand, we are not worried. On coarse sand, we are worried. On road dust, we are worried. On straw that was tied into a bundle, we are worried. If the straw was not bundled, we are not worried.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues its list of surfaces a falling bird might land on. For each one it says whether we must worry that the fall shattered its insides.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same material can get different rulings depending on its condition. Fine sand is fine, but coarse sand is not. Loose straw is fine, but bundled straw is not. A surface that gives way softens the fall, while a firm, packed surface does not.

keyTerms.meaning: We are concerned (here, that the bird's insides were shattered)
Dust of the road (packed and hard)

steps.confusionAlert: 'We are concerned' does not mean the bird is automatically a טרפה. It means there is a worry of רסוק אברים that has to be dealt with. 'Not concerned' means the fall itself raises no problem.

phrases.english: Fine sand: we are not concerned;
phrases.notes: 'Concerned' means worried that the bird's insides got shattered when it fell.

phrases.english: coarse sand: we are concerned;
dust of the roads: we are concerned;
straw that was made into a bundle: we are concerned;
if it was not made into a bundle: we are not concerned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of falling surfaces from the earlier part of the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Fine sand and loose straw: no concern. Coarse sand, road dust and bundled straw: concern of רסוק אברים.

steps.title: Grains and beans
steps.stepSummary: Wheat and barley types raise a worry. Most beans (קטניות) do not, except רוביא. חמצי raise no worry, but חפצי do.
steps.simpleTranslation: Wheat and everything like it: we are worried. Barley and everything like it: we are worried. All kinds of beans raise no worry of shattered limbs, except fenugreek. Peas raise no worry of shattered limbs; chickpeas do.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps going through its list, now covering a bird that fell onto piles of grain or beans.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Grains like wheat and barley count as hard surfaces, so there is a worry. Beans are generally safe. The גמרא then names exceptions: רוביא among the beans, and חפצי, which raise a worry even though חמצי do not.

keyTerms.meaning: Shattering of the limbs or internal organs, which makes the bird a טרפה

phrases.english: Wheat and all its types: we are concerned;
barley and all its types: we are concerned;
all types of legumes:
they raise no concern of shattered limbs,
except for fenugreek.

phrases.aramaic: חִימְצֵי – אֵין בּוֹ מִשּׁוּם רִיסּוּק אֵבָרִים,
phrases.english: Peas: there is no concern of shattered limbs,

phrases.aramaic: חִפְצֵי – יֵשׁ בּוֹ מִשּׁוּם רִיסּוּק אֵבָרִים.
phrases.english: chickpeas: there is a concern of shattered limbs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of surfaces, moving from ground materials to grains and beans.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wheat and barley types: concern. Beans: no concern, except רוביא. חמצי: no concern. חפצי: concern.

steps.title: The general rule: does the surface slip away?
steps.stepSummary: Anything that slips away under the bird raises no worry. Anything that does not slip raises a worry of רסוק אברים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The general rule is: anything that slips away raises no concern of shattered limbs. Anything that does not slip away raises a concern of shattered limbs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wraps up the whole list with one simple test that explains every case before it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of memorizing each material, you ask one question: does it slide out from under the bird? If it does, the fall is softened and there is no worry. If it stays firm, the bird hits something solid and we worry about רסוק אברים.

keyTerms.meaning: The general rule of the matter
Slips or slides away (gives way on impact)

steps.whatToRemember: The test for a falling bird is whether the surface slips away. If it slips, there is no worry. If it stays firm, there is a worry of רסוק אברים.
steps.whyThisMatters: This principle lets you decide surfaces the list never mentions.

phrases.english: The general rule of the matter:
anything that slips away:
there is no concern of shattered limbs,

phrases.aramaic: לָא מַשְׁרֵיק – יֵשׁ בּוֹ מִשּׁוּם רִיסּוּק אֵבָרִים.
phrases.english: does not slip away: there is a concern of shattered limbs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Summarizes all the listed cases with one principle.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A surface that slips away raises no worry of רסוק אברים. A firm surface does.

steps.title: A bird stuck to a glue-board: רב אשי versus אמימר
steps.stepSummary: About a bird that fell while stuck to a glue-board (דבוק), רב אשי permits it and אמימר forbids it.
steps.simpleTranslation: A glue-board: רב אשי permitted, and אמימר forbade.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new case: a bird caught on a glue-board that fell. It simply states the dispute, setting up the next step, which explains what exactly they argue about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether a bird stuck to the board could soften its own fall. רב אשי says the bird is permitted and אמימר says it is forbidden. The next steps define when each one applies.

keyTerms.meaning: A glue-board or sticky trap for catching birds

phrases.english: A glue-board: Rav Ashi permitted,
phrases.notes: This is a bird caught on a sticky board that fell to the ground while still stuck to it.

phrases.english: Ameimar forbade.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּבוֹק – רַב אָשֵׁי שָׁרֵי, אַמֵּימָר אָסַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from types of surfaces to a new case: a bird stuck to a trap.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a dispute: רב אשי permits a bird that fell stuck to a glue-board, and אמימר forbids it.

steps.title: First version: they argue only when both wings are stuck
steps.stepSummary: With one wing stuck, everyone permits. They argue when both wings are stuck: can the bird prop itself up on its wing-tips?
steps.simpleTranslation: With one wing stuck, everyone agrees it is permitted. They argue when two wings are stuck. The one who forbids says: how could it stand itself up? The one who permits says: it can stand on the tips of its wings.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the exact case of the dispute and gives each side's reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This narrows the dispute to two stuck wings. With only one wing stuck, everyone permits. The argument is whether a bird with both wings stuck can still hold itself up enough to soften the fall. The one who forbids says it cannot. The one who permits says it can, using its wing-tips.

keyTerms.meaning: Everyone agrees (literally, all the world does not argue)
The tips or ends of the wings

phrases.aramaic: בְּחַד גַּפָּא – דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי דִּשְׁרֵי,
phrases.english: With one wing, everyone agrees that it is permitted,
where they argue is with two wings.

phrases.aramaic: מַאן דְּאָסַר אָמַר לָךְ: הֵיכִי נֵיקוּם?
phrases.english: The one who forbids can tell you: how can it stand itself up?
And the one who permits can tell you:
it is possible for it to stand on the tips of the wings.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּחַד גַּפָּא – דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי דִּשְׁרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the case and the reasoning behind the רב אשי and אמימר dispute.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One wing stuck: permitted by all. Two wings stuck: disputed, depending on whether the bird can stand on its wing-tips.

steps.title: Second version: they argue only when one wing is stuck
steps.stepSummary: Another version says two stuck wings are forbidden by all. The argument is about one stuck wing: can the bird fly with the free wing?
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: with two wings stuck, everyone agrees it is forbidden. They argue about one wing. The one who permits says it can fly with one wing. The one who forbids says: since it cannot fly with this wing, it cannot fly with that one either.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different version of where רב אשי and אמימר disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This version moves the dispute down a level. Two stuck wings are forbidden by everyone, and the argument is over one stuck wing. The one who permits says the free wing is enough to soften the fall. The one who forbids says one wing alone cannot fly, so the bird fell hard.
steps.confusionAlert: Both versions are about the same two sages. Only the case they argue about changes. In the first version they argue over two wings, and in the second over one wing.

phrases.english: And there are those who say:

phrases.aramaic: בִּתְרֵי גַּפֵּי כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי דַּאֲסִיר,
phrases.english: with two wings, everyone agrees that it is forbidden,
where they argue is with one wing.
The one who permits can tell you:
it is possible that it flies with one wing,
and the one who forbids says:
since with this one it cannot fly,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the wing stuck to the board.

phrases.english: with that one it also cannot fly.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different version of the dispute from step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two wings stuck: forbidden by all. One wing stuck: disputed, depending on whether a bird can fly with one wing.

steps.title: The final הלכה: two wings forbidden, one wing permitted
steps.stepSummary: The הלכה is that a bird stuck by two wings is forbidden, and one stuck by one wing is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the הלכה is: with two wings stuck, it is forbidden. With one wing stuck, it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the practical ruling for the glue-board case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ruling fits the parts both versions agree on. In the first version everyone permits one wing, and in the second everyone forbids two wings. So the הלכה is: one wing permitted, two wings forbidden.
steps.whatToRemember: For a bird that fell stuck to a glue-board: two wings stuck, it is forbidden; one wing stuck, it is permitted.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practical ruling for a common way birds were trapped.

phrases.english: And the halacha is:
with two wings, it is forbidden,
with one wing, it is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the dispute after both versions have been given.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A bird with two wings stuck to a glue-board is forbidden. With one wing stuck, it is permitted.

steps.title: What counts as most of the ribs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of broken ribs, and a ברייתא explains that 'most of the ribs' means twelve: six on each side, or eleven on one side and one on the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: if most of its ribs were broken, it is a טרפה. The Rabbis taught: 'Most of the ribs' means six from this side and six from that side, or eleven from one side and one from the other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic from the משנה, broken ribs, and a ברייתא defines exactly how many ribs make up 'most.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: An animal has eleven important ribs on each side, twenty-two in total. Twelve is a majority, so any combination that reaches twelve counts. It does not matter whether the breaks are spread evenly or nearly all on one side.

keyTerms.meaning: Most of the ribs, a majority of the ribs
An animal with a fatal defect, which is forbidden to eat even after שחיטה
From here, meaning from one side of the animal

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the basic number, twelve broken ribs, that the rest of the סוגיא builds on and refines.

phrases.english: If most of its ribs were broken.
The Rabbis taught:
These are 'most of the ribs':
six from here and six from there,
phrases.notes: 'Here' and 'there' mean the two sides of the animal.

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ אַחַת עֶשְׂרֵה מִכָּאן וְאַחַת מִכָּאן.
phrases.english: or eleven from here and one from there.
phrases.notes: There are eleven ribs on each side, twenty-two in all, so twelve is a majority either way.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֵלּוּ הֵן רוֹב צְלָעוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the bird and glue-board discussion and opens the משנה's next case, broken ribs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Most of the ribs means twelve of twenty-two, in any split between the two sides.

steps.title: Only breaks on the half near the spine count
steps.stepSummary: זעירי adds that the broken ribs count only if the break is on the half of the rib closer to the spine.
steps.simpleTranslation: זעירי said: And this is only when they broke in the half that is toward the spine.
steps.whatsHappening: זעירי narrows the ברייתא's rule. Not every break counts, only a break on the spine-side half of the rib.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gave a number, twelve, but did not say where on the rib the break has to be. זעירי adds a location rule: breaks on the outer half, away from the spine, are not counted toward the twelve.

keyTerms.meaning: From their half, meaning the half of each rib

phrases.english: Ze'eiri said:
And from their half toward the spine.
phrases.notes: He means a break counts only if it is on the half of the rib closer to the spine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a limit on where the break must be for the twelve-rib rule of step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only breaks on the spine-side half of a rib count toward most of the ribs.

steps.title: Only the large ribs with marrow count
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן adds a second limit: the rule is about the large ribs that contain marrow.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: And this is about the large ribs that have marrow in them.
steps.whatsHappening: Another אמורא narrows the rule further. Only the big ribs with marrow inside count, not the small ribs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: זעירי limited where on the rib the break must be. רבי יוחנן limits which ribs count at all: the large, marrow-filled ones. Breaks in small ribs do not count toward the twelve.

keyTerms.meaning: Marrow, the soft material inside the bone

phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Chana said
Rabbi Yochanan said:
And in large ribs
that have marrow in them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: וּבִצְלָעוֹת גְּדוֹלוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second limit on the rule of step 8, this time about which ribs count.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only large ribs that contain marrow count toward most of the ribs.
steps.whatToRemember: Three conditions so far: twelve ribs, broken on the half near the spine, and only the large marrow-filled ribs.

steps.title: Uprooted ribs need only most of one side
steps.stepSummary: עולא quotes בן זכאי: if ribs were uprooted from the spine, most of one side is enough; if they were broken, most of both sides is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said that בן זכאי said: If they were uprooted, most of one side is enough. If they were broken, it must be most of both sides.
steps.whatsHappening: A new statement compares two kinds of damage. Ribs pulled out of the spine are treated as more serious than ribs that are broken.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far we only spoke about broken ribs. בן זכאי says uprooted ribs are worse, so six uprooted ribs on one side already make a טרפה. Broken ribs still need twelve, counted across both sides.

keyTerms.meaning: Were uprooted, pulled out from where they attach to the spine

steps.confusionAlert: 'Uprooted' and 'broken' are two different injuries. Uprooted means the rib came out of its joint at the spine; broken means the bone itself snapped.

phrases.english: Ulla said,
Ben Zakkai said:
If they were uprooted — with most of one side;
if they were broken — with most of both sides.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר עוּלָּא, בֶּן זַכַּאי אָמַר: נֶעְקְרוּ – בְּרוֹב צַד אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings in a new kind of injury, uprooted ribs, and compares it to the broken ribs of step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Uprooted ribs make a טרפה with most of one side; broken ribs need most of both sides.

steps.title: Uprooted or broken, both sides are needed
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן disagrees: whether the ribs were uprooted or broken, it takes most of both sides.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: Whether they were uprooted or whether they were broken, it must be most of both sides.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן argues with בן זכאי and treats uprooted ribs exactly like broken ribs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בן זכאי gave uprooted ribs a lower number, six on one side. רבי יוחנן says there is no difference. Both injuries need twelve ribs counted across both sides.

keyTerms.meaning: Whether... or, covering both cases the same way

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
Whether they were uprooted or broken —
with most of both sides.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר: בֵּין נֶעְקְרוּ בֵּין נִשְׁתַּבְּרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing opinion to בן זכאי in step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Uprooted and broken ribs are the same: both need most of both sides.
steps.whatToRemember: בן זכאי: uprooted needs only most of one side. רבי יוחנן: uprooted or broken, always most of both sides.

steps.title: A rib uprooted together with its vertebra
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that if even one rib was uprooted and a vertebra came out with it, the animal is a טרפה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: If a rib was uprooted and a vertebra came out with it, it is a טרפה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב gives a new case: even a single uprooted rib makes a טרפה if a piece of the spine came out along with it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now we needed many ribs. Here one rib is enough, because the damage reaches the spine itself. The vertebra coming out is what makes this case so serious.

keyTerms.meaning: A vertebra, one of the bones of the spine

phrases.english: Rav said:
If a rib was uprooted and a vertebra with it —
it is a tereifa.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: נֶעֶקְרָה צֵלָע וְחוּלְיָא עִמָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from counting many uprooted ribs to a single rib uprooted together with its vertebra.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One rib uprooted along with its vertebra makes the animal a טרפה.

steps.title: Two ribs uprooted from one vertebra
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא and רב אסי ask רב about two ribs uprooted from the same vertebra, one on each side, while the vertebra itself stays in place.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא and רב אסי said to רב: If a rib was uprooted from this side and a rib from that side, and the vertebra stays in place, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: Two students ask רב a follow-up question about his rule. The גמרא is setting up רב's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רב's case the vertebra came out. Here the vertebra stays, but both ribs attached to it are gone. They want to know if that still makes a טרפה.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרִי לֵיהּ רַב כָּהֲנָא וְרַב אַסִּי לְרַב:
phrases.english: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi said to Rav:
If a rib was uprooted from here and a rib from there,
phrases.notes: These are the two ribs attached to the same vertebra, one on each side.

phrases.english: and the vertebra stays in place, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי לֵיהּ רַב כָּהֲנָא וְרַב אַסִּי לְרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks a follow-up on רב's rule in step 13, changing the case so the vertebra stays.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is an animal a טרפה when both ribs of one vertebra are uprooted but the vertebra stays in place?

steps.title: This is like an animal cut in half
steps.stepSummary: רב answers with surprise: are you asking about an animal that is split in half? Of course it is not kosher.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Are you talking about an animal that is cut in two?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers that the question is obvious. Losing both ribs of one vertebra is like the animal being sliced in half.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The students thought keeping the vertebra might help. רב says it does not: with the rib on each side of the vertebra torn away, the animal is like it was split in two. That is even worse than his own case, so it is certainly forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: Something split or cut in half
Are you saying? Are you talking about?

steps.whatToRemember: One rib plus its vertebra uprooted makes a טרפה. Both ribs of one vertebra uprooted is like an animal cut in half, which is certainly forbidden.

phrases.english: He said to them:
Are you talking about an animal cut in two?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The animal is like one cut in half, so it is obviously forbidden, even though the vertebra stays in place.

steps.title: Isn't רב's own earlier case also a split animal?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב: his earlier case of a rib uprooted together with a vertebra should also count as a גיסטרא.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't רב also describe a split animal in his earlier ruling?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question on רב. His earlier case, a rib uprooted with its vertebra, seems to be the same as a split animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 13 רב said that a rib uprooted with a vertebra makes the animal a טרפה. If the whole vertebra comes out, the rib on the other side comes loose too, so the animal is split in half. In step 15 רב said a split animal is not kosher at all, which is worse than טרפה, so his two rulings seem to clash.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal that is split or sliced in half; treated as a dead animal (נבלה), not just a טרפה
'But isn't it so that...', a word that opens a challenge
An animal with a fatal injury; forbidden to eat even after proper שחיטה
An animal treated as already dead; a more severe status than טרפה

steps.confusionAlert: Keep the two levels apart. A טרפה is a fatally injured animal, but a גיסטרא is treated like it is already dead. רב gave the milder label in step 13 and the harsher one in step 15.

phrases.english: But didn't רב also
describe a split animal?
phrases.notes: This points back to step 13. If a whole vertebra comes out, the rib across from it comes loose too, so the animal is split.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses רב's answer in step 15 to challenge his own ruling in step 13
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling in step 13 (rib plus vertebra is a טרפה)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A whole vertebra coming out frees both sides, which is a גיסטרא. רב himself says a גיסטרא is not kosher at all, not merely a טרפה.

steps.title: רב meant a rib without the vertebra
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא first answers that רב's טרפה ruling was about a rib uprooted without its vertebra.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב said it, he meant a rib without a vertebra.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by changing how we read רב's earlier ruling. He was talking about a rib that came out alone, without the vertebra.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If no vertebra came out, the other side stays attached, so the animal is not split. That would explain why רב called it only a טרפה and not a גיסטרא.

keyTerms.meaning: Vertebra, one segment of the spine
'When he said it...', a phrase that explains what someone really meant

phrases.english: When רב said it,
he meant a rib without a vertebra.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי קָאָמַר רַב צֵלָע בְּלֹא חוּלְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב's טרפה case included a whole vertebra coming out
steps.terutzMaskana: רב's טרפה case was only a rib, with no vertebra

steps.title: But רב explicitly mentioned a vertebra
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects that reading, because רב clearly spoke about a rib together with a vertebra.
steps.simpleTranslation: But he said 'a rib and a vertebra'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer. רב's own words in step 13 mention a vertebra coming out with the rib.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An answer cannot contradict the plain words of the ruling. Since רב said the vertebra came out, 'a rib without a vertebra' does not work.

keyTerms.meaning: A rib together with a vertebra, the wording of רב's ruling

phrases.english: But he said a rib and a vertebra!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the answer of step 17 based on רב's exact wording
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב's words explicitly include a vertebra, so his case cannot be a rib without one.

steps.title: A rib with half a vertebra
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רב meant a rib that came out together with half of its vertebra.
steps.simpleTranslation: He meant a rib and half a vertebra.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new answer. Only half the vertebra came out with the rib, so the other side is still held in place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This keeps רב's word 'vertebra' and still avoids a split animal. The rib on the other side stays attached to the remaining half of the vertebra, so the animal is a טרפה, not a גיסטרא.

keyTerms.meaning: An answer that resolves a challenge

phrases.english: He meant a rib and half a vertebra.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 18 with a middle reading
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A rib with a vertebra means the whole vertebra came out, which would be a split animal
steps.terutzMaskana: Only half the vertebra came out, so the other side is intact and the animal is only a טרפה
steps.whatToRemember: רב's two rulings fit together: a rib with half a vertebra is a טרפה, while an animal truly split across both sides is a גיסטרא.

steps.title: How can two ribs make a split animal?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא infers that the question in step 14 was about ribs without the vertebra, and challenges this from בן זכאי's ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: So רב כהנא and רב אסי must have asked about ribs without the vertebra, and רב still called it a split animal? But עולא quoted בן זכאי: uprooted ribs need most of one side, and broken ribs need most of both sides.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a conclusion from the last answer and then challenges it. If רב's ruling covered half a vertebra, then the case asked about in step 14 had no vertebra damage at all. Yet רב called it a split animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בן זכאי says uprooted ribs make an animal a טרפה only if most of one side is uprooted. So two uprooted ribs should not even make it a טרפה. How could רב call it a גיסטרא, which is even worse?

keyTerms.meaning: 'From this we can infer...', drawing a conclusion from what was just said
Were uprooted, pulled out from the spine
Most of one side, meaning most of the ribs on one side

phrases.english: This implies that רב כהנא and רב אסי
were asking about ribs without the vertebra,
phrases.notes: Their question was in step 14: two ribs, one on each side, while the vertebra stayed in place.

phrases.english: and he answered them, 'Are you talking about a split animal?'
But didn't עולא say that בן זכאי said:
if the ribs were uprooted, it takes most of one side,
if they were broken, it takes most of both sides.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִכְּלָל דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא וְרַב אַסִּי צֵלָע בְּלֹא חוּלְיָא אָמְרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a conclusion from the answer in step 19 and attacks רב's reply in step 15
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's reply in step 15 that two uprooted ribs make a split animal
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under בן זכאי, uprooted ribs need most of one side even to be a טרפה. Two ribs should therefore be kosher, not a גיסטרא.

steps.title: Ribs facing each other are different
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that בן זכאי was speaking about ribs that are not across from each other, while רב's case had two ribs directly opposite each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב could tell you: there, the ribs are not across from each other; here, they are across from each other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for רב by telling the two cases apart. בן זכאי's rule is about ribs that do not line up, and רב's case is two ribs facing each other on the same vertebra.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When two ribs on opposite sides of the same vertebra are both pulled out, that spot of the body is cut through from side to side. That is what makes it a split animal, even with only two ribs. Many ribs on one side, or ribs that do not line up, do not split the body, so בן זכאי needs most of a side.

keyTerms.meaning: There, the other case being compared
Here, the case we are discussing
One across from the other, ribs directly opposite each other on both sides

steps.whatToRemember: How many ribs are uprooted is not the only thing that matters; where they are matters too. Two ribs directly opposite each other make a split animal (גיסטרא), while ribs that are not opposite each other follow בן זכאי's 'most of one side' rule.

phrases.english: He could tell you:
phrases.notes: 'He' is רב. This is what he could answer.

phrases.english: there, the ribs are not across from each other,
here, they are across from each other.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָךְ הָתָם זֶה שֶׁלֹּא כְּנֶגֶד זֶה הָכָא זֶה כְּנֶגֶד זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 20
steps.terutzHavaAmina: בן זכאי's 'most of one side' covers every case of uprooted ribs
steps.terutzMaskana: בן זכאי's rule covers ribs not across from each other; two ribs directly opposite each other make a split animal

steps.title: Challenge from רבי יוחנן's majority rule
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer in step 21. רבי יוחנן requires a majority of ribs on both sides, and such a majority must include two ribs opposite each other, yet he calls the animal only a טרפה, not a split animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't רבי יוחנן say the rule applies only when a majority of the ribs on both sides were torn out? With a majority on both sides, some pair is bound to be opposite each other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer it just gave, that two ribs opposite each other are a special case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן says a majority of ribs on both sides makes the animal a טרפה. Any such majority must include at least one pair of opposite ribs. By step 21's logic, that pair should make the animal a גיסטרא, treated as already dead, yet רבי יוחנן calls it only a טרפה.

keyTerms.meaning: both sides (of the spine / rib cage)

phrases.english: But didn't Rabbi Yochanan say:
[it applies only] with a majority of both sides,
and with a majority of both sides
it is impossible that there will not be
one pair of them opposite each other!
phrases.notes: Some versions read חד and the corrected wording reads חדא. Both mean "one".

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the step 21 answer that opposite ribs are a separate, special case.
steps.kashyaTarget: The distinction between ribs opposite each other and ribs not opposite each other (step 21).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן's majority always includes an opposite pair, yet he calls the animal only a טרפה, not a גיסטרא. So an opposite pair alone cannot be what makes an animal a גיסטרא.

steps.title: Pestle without mortar versus pestle with mortar
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן is speaking about the end of the rib pulled out while the vertebra stays whole. רב's case is a rib torn out together with part of the vertebra.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, the rib's end came out without its socket. Here, the rib's end came out together with its socket.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the two rulings are about different kinds of injuries.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When only the rib comes out and the spine stays whole, you need a majority of ribs, even though that majority includes an opposite pair. When the rib takes part of the vertebra with it, the spine itself is damaged, so two opposite ribs are a more serious case.

keyTerms.meaning: pestle: the rounded end of the rib
mortar: the socket in the vertebra where the rib sits
there / here: contrasting the two cases

phrases.english: There, the pestle came out without the mortar,
phrases.notes: "There" is רבי יוחנן's case. The rib's end is pictured as a pestle sitting in a mortar, which is the socket in the spine.

phrases.english: here, the pestle came out with the mortar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: the two rulings are about different injuries.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Two opposite ribs and רבי יוחנן's majority seemed to be the same kind of injury.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יוחנן is speaking about ribs without the vertebra. רב is speaking about ribs together with the vertebra.

steps.title: Wasn't the question already answered by רב?
steps.stepSummary: If the case asked about involves the vertebra, it seems to be the same as רב's own ruling, so why did they need to ask רב?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, isn't this the same as רב's ruling?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רב כהנא and רב אסי asked רב anything, if their case was already covered by his ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב already ruled that one rib torn out with half its vertebra makes the animal טרפה. Two opposite ribs with the vertebra should be טרפה all the more so. So the question seems unnecessary.

phrases.english: If so, that is the same as Rav's ruling?
phrases.notes: This points back to רב's ruling in step 13, read in step 19 as a rib torn out with half its vertebra.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the answer of step 23 to raise a new difficulty about the question in step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for the question asked of רב in step 14.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב's ruling on one rib with its vertebra already covers two ribs with the vertebra, all the more so. So the question was unnecessary.

steps.title: They had not heard רב's ruling
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא and רב אסי did not know about רב's ruling, so they had to ask.
steps.simpleTranslation: They had not heard רב's ruling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers simply that the people asking did not know רב's earlier ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is not unnecessary in principle. The people asking just lacked the information.

phrases.english: They had not heard Rav's ruling.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The people asking did not know the earlier ruling.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Their question seemed already answered by רב's ruling.
steps.terutzMaskana: They asked because they did not know רב's ruling.

steps.title: Why not ask about the simpler case?
steps.stepSummary: If they did not know רב's ruling, they should have asked about the simpler case of one rib with its vertebra, as רב discussed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let them ask him about the case רב discussed!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why they chose to ask about two opposite ribs instead of the basic case of one rib.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The natural question would be about one rib torn out with its vertebra. Asking about two opposite ribs seems to skip the basic question.

phrases.english: Then let them ask him about the case like Rav's?
phrases.notes: He means the case of just one rib with half its vertebra, the case רב ruled on.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the answer in step 25 to question how the question was worded.
steps.kashyaTarget: The choice to ask about two opposite ribs.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If they did not know the basic ruling, the logical thing would be to ask about the basic one-rib case.

steps.title: One question that teaches two cases
steps.stepSummary: They asked about two ribs because that question would teach them about both cases. Asking about one rib might leave the two-rib case still unanswered.
steps.simpleTranslation: They reasoned: let us ask him one question that will explain two cases to us. If we ask about one rib and he says טרפה, then two ribs are surely טרפה. But if he says כשרה, we would still need to ask about two ribs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the smart reasoning behind how they worded their question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ruling of טרפה for one rib would cover two ribs all the more so. A ruling of כשרה for one rib would not settle the two-rib case. Asking about two ribs seemed to avoid that problem, but the next step challenges this reasoning.

keyTerms.meaning: an animal with a fatal defect, which may not be eaten

steps.whatToRemember: Ribs pulled out without the vertebra need a majority on both sides (רבי יוחנן). When the vertebra comes out too, even one rib can be enough (רב). The question about two opposite ribs was worded so that one answer would teach about both cases.

phrases.english: They reasoned:
Let us ask him one question
that will explain two cases to us,
for if we ask him about one,
phrases.notes: "One" means one rib torn out with its vertebra, and "two" means two opposite ribs.

phrases.english: that works if he tells us "טרפה":
all the more so with two;
but if he tells us "kosher,"
we still have a question about two.

steps.triggerLanguage: סָבְרִי: לִיבְעֵי מִינֵּיהּ חֲדָא דְּפָרֵישׁ לַן תַּרְתֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the strategy behind the wording: one question covering two cases.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Asking about the one-rib case seemed more logical.
steps.terutzMaskana: Asking about two ribs guarantees an answer covering both cases, but asking about one rib might not.

steps.title: Asking about two ribs might still leave one question open
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the last answer. Asking about two ribs only teaches both cases if רב answers 'kosher'. If he answers 'טרפה', the one-rib case is still unknown.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, then even now that they asked about two ribs, it only works if he said 'kosher', because then one rib is surely kosher. But if he said 'טרפה', they would still have a question about one rib.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from step 27, which said asking about two ribs covers both cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A 'kosher' answer for two ribs proves one rib is kosher too (כל שכן). But a 'טרפה' answer for two ribs proves nothing about one rib. So asking about two does not always cover both cases, and step 27's reasoning seems to fail.

keyTerms.meaning: an animal with a fatal injury, forbidden to eat

phrases.english: If so,

phrases.aramaic: הַשְׁתָּא נָמֵי דְּקָא בָּעֵי מִינֵּיהּ תַּרְתֵּי,
phrases.english: now too, when they ask him about two ribs,
it works out well if he tells them 'kosher'
then all the more so with one rib;
but if he tells them 'טרפה',
they still have a question about one rib.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 27
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that asking about two ribs teaches both cases
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The two-rib question only settles the one-rib case if the answer is 'kosher'. If the answer is 'טרפה', the one-rib case stays open.

steps.title: If one rib were enough, רב would have gotten angry
steps.stepSummary: The students reasoned that if one rib already made the animal טרפה, רב would get angry at a question about two. So whatever answer he gave would still teach them something.
steps.simpleTranslation: They reasoned: if so, he would surely get angry and say, 'If one rib is already טרפה, do you need to ask about two?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 28 by showing that רב's reaction itself would give them the information.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If one rib were enough for טרפה, asking about two would be a pointless question, and רב would show anger. So a calm 'טרפה' answer would mean one rib is not טרפה. Either way, they learn about both cases.

keyTerms.meaning: is it a question? does it need to be asked?

phrases.aramaic: סָבְרִי: אִם כֵּן מִירְתָּח קָא רָתַח.
phrases.english: They reasoned: if so, he would surely get angry.
phrases.notes: 'If so' means: if רב holds that even one rib makes the animal טרפה.

phrases.english: 'If one is טרפה, do you need to ask about two?'

steps.triggerLanguage: סָבְרִי: אִם כֵּן מִירְתָּח קָא רָתַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 28
steps.terutzResolutionType: The teacher's reaction would itself give the missing information
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A 'טרפה' answer about two ribs leaves the one-rib case unknown
steps.terutzMaskana: If one rib were already טרפה, רב would react with anger, so the students would learn about the one-rib case either way

steps.title: But they asked, and רב did not get angry
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that the students did ask about two ribs and רב did not get angry, even though he holds that one rib makes the animal טרפה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But they did ask him, and he did not get angry!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 29 using what actually happened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier in the סוגיא we saw that רב holds even one rib makes the animal טרפה. By step 29's logic, he should have gotten angry. Since the story shows no anger, step 29's answer seems not to fit the facts.

keyTerms.meaning: and he did not get angry

phrases.english: But they did say it to him
and he did not get angry,

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא קָא אָמְרִי לֵיהּ וְלָא רָתַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 29 from the actual story
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רב would have shown anger
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב holds one rib is טרפה, yet when asked about two he did not show anger, so the theory does not match what happened.

steps.title: 'Are you talking about a sliced animal?' was his anger
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רב's sharp reply, 'Are you talking about an animal sliced in half?', was his anger. From it the students learned that two ribs opposite each other is like a split animal, a נבלה, while one rib is טרפה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since he said to them, 'Are you talking about an animal sliced in half?', that was his anger.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that רב did react with anger, just in a quiet, sharp way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's reply was a rebuke: two ribs torn opposite each other is like an animal cut in two. That tone was his anger. So the students learned both cases: two ribs make it a נבלה, and one rib makes it a טרפה.

keyTerms.meaning: an animal that counts as already dead, a carcass

steps.whatToRemember: The students asked about two ribs on purpose. רב's sharp reply about a 'sliced' animal taught them that two opposite ribs is a נבלה, and one rib is a טרפה.
steps.confusionAlert: רב's reply was not a calm answer. The 'sliced animal' remark was itself the anger the students were watching for.

phrases.english: Since he said to them, 'Are you talking about a sliced animal?'
that was his anger.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיוָן דְּקָאָמַר לְהוּ ״גִּיסְטְרָא קָאָמְרִיתוּ״ – הַיְינוּ רִיתְחֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 30 and closes the discussion about the students' question
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines what counted as רב's anger
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב answered calmly and showed no anger
steps.terutzMaskana: His sharp 'sliced animal' reply was the anger, so they learned that two ribs make a נבלה and one rib makes a טרפה

steps.title: שמואל's three cases of טרפה
steps.stepSummary: A new statement of שמואל, passed on through רב מתנא and רבה בר רב שילא, lists three injuries that make an animal טרפה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב שילא said in the name of רב מתנא, who said it in the name of שמואל: a rib torn out from its root, a skull crushed in most of it, and the flesh covering most of the rumen damaged in most of it all make the animal טרפה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic with a ruling of שמואל listing three injuries that make an animal טרפה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each case has its own measure. The rib must be torn from its root, the skull must be crushed in its majority, and the flesh over the rumen must be damaged in its majority. The phrase 'its majority' sets the amount of damage needed.

keyTerms.meaning: from its root, where it attaches

steps.whyThisMatters: This statement sets three new standards for טרפה, which the גמרא will go on to discuss.

phrases.english: רבה בר רב שילא said
that רב מתנא said that שמואל said:
If a rib was torn out from its root,
or a skull that was crushed in most of it,
or the flesh that covers most of the rumen
was damaged in most of it, the animal is טרפה.
phrases.notes: The word 'damaged' is not in the text; the גמרא leaves it out but means it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר רַב שֵׁילָא אָמַר רַב מַתְנָא אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new statement after the discussion of רב's ruling ends
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A rib torn from its root, a skull crushed in its majority, and the flesh covering most of the rumen damaged in its majority all make the animal טרפה

steps.title: Questioning the torn-out rib ruling
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether a rib torn out from its root really makes an animal טרפה, and announces a contradicting source.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it really true that if a rib was torn out from its root, the animal is טרפה? Here is a source that seems to contradict this:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא picks one item from שמואל's list, the torn-out rib, and doubts it. This line is a setup: it announces that a contradicting source is about to be quoted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 32 listed three injuries that make an animal טרפה. The גמרא now focuses only on the rib case. The word ורמינהו tells us another source seems to treat this case differently, and that source is quoted at the start of the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: from its root, its base where it joins the spine
an animal with a deadly injury, forbidden to eat even after proper שחיטה
"And they threw them against each other": a source that seems to contradict is about to be quoted

steps.confusionAlert: This line does not yet say what the contradiction is. It only questions שמואל's ruling and announces that a contradicting source is coming next.

phrases.english: A rib was torn out from its root, it is a tereifa?
phrases.notes: This is one of the three injuries שמואל listed in the previous step. The גמרא is asking, "Did he really say that?"

phrases.english: But raise a contradiction:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges one of the three טרפה injuries listed in שמואל's statement in Step 32.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling that a rib torn out from its root makes the animal טרפה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another source seems to contradict this ruling. The source is quoted on the next amud, where the exact clash is shown.
